2018_121_051518regmtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education regular meeting of May 15, 2018, held at Athens High School. It is the district's leadership-turnover meeting: nine administrative appointments in a single sitting — a finance director, three other directors, a special education supervisor and four principals, at Hill, Baker, Boulan Park and Smith — set against a retiree list of nearly thirty employees, several with careers going back to 1974 and 1979. It also recognizes 17 Outstanding Support Staff nominees, awards $650,000.00 of sinking-fund flooring and $37,645.00 of asbestos abatement, and expresses the statutory support required for Oakland Schools' $320.7 million FY 2019 budget.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting, May 15, 2018, 7:00 PM, **Athens High School, 4333 John R** — not the usual Services Building.

**Recognition**
Four items. The Mission Moment honors the Facilities Study Attendance Area Review Team — Lori Bluhm, Emily Cremers, Laura Duzey, Jeff Frederick, Victoria King, Veronica Pala, Delia Rodi-Barczys, Lori Sisk and Courtney Spangler — along with administrative liaisons Mark Dziatczak and Kris Griffor.

Seventeen support staff were nominated for the Outstanding Support Staff Award, chosen by colleagues, parents and students "because they make a difference for our students each and every day… when we say we ensure learning for all - ALL truly means ALL." **Tina Houser, health care aide at Morse Elementary, is named Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year** and her name forwarded to the county.

The retiree list runs to nearly thirty names, the longest-tenured being Cindy Kolesar (Hamilton, since 1974), Janice Brzezinski (Hill, since 1979) and Nancy Schleicher (Hamilton, since 1979). The staging is spelled out: monitors display a visual recognition for twenty minutes before the meeting, Jordan Harris reads each name, position and length of career, and President Karl Schmidt presents each retiree a clock. The fourth item adopts a resolution supporting National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 7-11, 2018.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the April 10 workshop and April 17 meeting, the March 2018 Treasurer's Report, and approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget for 2018-2019.

**Treasurer's Report — March 2018**
Total check disbursements are $7,613,150.06, the General Fund group $4,993,833.82 and the General Fund (101) itself $4,631,730.82. With $3,354,883.06 of wire transfers, $172,373.08 of P-Card purchases and $70,536.47 of ACH debits, total disbursements in period are $11,210,942.67.

**Approving someone else's budget**
Section 624 of the Revised School Code requires the ISD to submit its proposed budget to each constituent district by May 1, and each constituent board to adopt a resolution expressing support or disapproval by June 1. Troy's resolution expresses support — and says exactly why it is doing so: the Board "believes that it is the responsibility of the Intermediate School District to be responsible for its own operations, including adoption of its budget," and Troy's support "is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624."

The attached overview shows Oakland Schools' FY 2019 revenue at **$320.7 million** — 58% property taxes ($186.2 million), 23% new grant awards ($73.0 million), 10% other local ($31.3 million), 5% state ($16.1 million), 3% grant carryover ($9.6 million) and 1% other financing sources ($4.5 million). Property tax collection is in its fifth year of recovery, but the FY 2019 levy of $186.2 million is still **$30.7 million below the FY 2008 base of $216.9 million**, with the gap not projected to close until FY 2023-24. Budget assumptions include a 3.4% property tax increase (including the probability of a Headlee rollback), a 1.25% salary increase plus roughly .5% of steps, a 3.9% health care cap increase and a blended MPSERS rate of **26.16%**. Countywide LEA membership has fallen from 199,713 in 2009 to 187,896 in 2018.

**Personnel — nine appointments, each a two-year contract**

| Position | Appointee | Coming from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finance Director | Kandice Moynihan | Walled Lake Consolidated Schools |
| Director, Employee Services | John Pagel | Martell Elementary principal |
| Director, Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment | Tim Fulcher | Smith Middle School principal |
| Special Education Supervisor | Sarah Young | TSD behavior support coordinator |
| Director, Early Childhood Programs | Erin Keyser | Morse preschool teacher |
| Principal, Hill Elementary | Shari Pawlus | Morse reading specialist |
| Principal, Baker Middle | Jonathan Cross | Baker assistant principal |
| Principal, Boulan Park Middle | Anthony Morse | Boulan Park assistant principal |
| Principal, Smith Middle | Christian Mueller | Utica Community Schools |

Seven of the nine are internal moves. Erin Keyser's appointment as Director of Early Childhood Programs staffs the leadership of the preschool the Board had just financed and put out to bid.

**Business**
Flooring replacement at Athens, IA East, Boulan Park, Larson, Bemis, Martell and Wass goes to **Conventional Carpet at $650,000.00** from the Building Site and Sinking Project Fund. Asbestos abatement of floor tile at Athens, IA East, Boulan Park, Larson and Wass — necessary in conjunction with the flooring project, per Rob Carson's April 26 memo on Bid 9858 — goes to **Abatement & Demolition Services at $37,645.00** from the same fund.

**Other**
The Oakland Schools Board of Education biennial election is June 4, 2018: two candidates, Dr. Theresa Rich and Mr. Marc Katz, for two six-year seats ending June 30, 2024. Each constituent district must designate one representative to the electoral body and direct their vote by resolution; no absentee ballots are accepted.

Agenda packet for the regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, May 15, 2018, 7:00 PM at Athens High School, 4333 John R — the Board meeting away from the Services Building for this one. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Recognition — A. TSD Mission Moment: Facilities Study Attendance Area Review Team, B. Outstanding Support Staff Person of the Year, C. Troy School District Retirees, D. Teacher Appreciation Week; 3. Additions & Deletions; 4. Public Communication (agenda items); 5. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the April 10, 2018 Board of Education Workshop, B. Minutes of the April 17, 2018 Board of Education Meeting, C. Treasurer's Report – March 2018, D. Approve Oakland Intermediate School District Budget for 2018-2019; 6. Personnel — A through I, nine administrative appointments; 7. Curriculum; 8. Business — A. Consideration: Sinking Fund Site Flooring Projects, B. Consideration: Asbestos Abatement; 9. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 10. Other — A. Consideration: Oakland Schools Board of Education Biennial Election; 11. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools.

**Recognition 2.A: the Facilities Study Attendance Area Review Team.** This year the district formed a Facilities Study Team Attendance Area Review Committee to conduct a comprehensive review of current attendance area patterns according to specific criteria: resolving double split learning pathways, examining enrollment across buildings to address overcrowding and imbalances within the classroom, and minimizing changes to school attendance areas across Troy. The team was made up of members of the community and the district's Pupil Accounting Coordinator; the individuals volunteered and gave countless hours of their time and expertise. Certificates go to Lori Bluhm, Emily Cremers, Laura Duzey, Jeff Frederick, Victoria King, Veronica Pala, Delia Rodi-Barczys, Lori Sisk and Courtney Spangler. The Board also recognizes Deputy Superintendent for Teaching & Learning Mark Dziatczak and Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction Kris Griffor, the administrative liaisons, noting that the district could not have undertaken a comprehensive study like this without their leadership and direction.

**Recognition 2.B: 2017-18 Outstanding Support Staff Award.** Seventeen individuals were nominated. The nominees were chosen by their colleagues, by parents and by former and current students, because they make a difference for students each and every day: "They exemplify our values and help us to ensure that when we say we ensure learning for all - ALL truly means ALL." The nominees are Tina Houser, health care aide, Morse Elementary; Mike Boussie, Safe Ed, Troy College and Career High School; Robert Dean, custodian, Hamilton Elementary; Jeannette Eve, Tier 1 program assistant, Troy Center for Transition; Keith Giacoma, health care aide, Wass Elementary; Karen Hilty, food service supervisor, Smith Middle School; Barb Johnson, secretary, Athletics; Kathy Koncagul, computer tech, Leonard Elementary; Sharon Kreza, secretary, Wattles Elementary; Garry Marble, custodian, Wattles Elementary; Nancy Mosey, paraprofessional, Barnard Elementary; Tony Recchia, bus driver, Hamilton Elementary; Majd Tominna, ELD paraprofessional, Troy High School; Meena Trivedi, ELD paraprofessional, Hamilton Elementary; Nancy Wells, computer tech, Athens High School; Austin Woodard, paraprofessional, Boulan Park Middle School; and Seth Wyatt, paraprofessional, Costello Elementary. From that pool, Tina Houser was awarded the Troy School District Outstanding Support Staff Employee of the Year, and her name was also sent to the county for consideration for the county-wide Outstanding Support Staff Award.

**Recognition 2.C: Troy School District retirees.** The item introduces employees who have retired or expressed their intention to retire at the end of the 2017-2018 school year, noting that not all could be present. The list: Anaam Asmar, paraprofessional, Martell, since 1997; Janice Brzezinski, administrator, Hill Elementary, since 1979; Karen Chick, teacher, Schroeder, since 1989; Kathleen Everlove, GSRP associate teacher, Troy Union, since 1999; Rebecca Haga, childhood supervisor, Niles Center, since 1986; Karen Hoffman, teacher, Services Building, since 1990; Linda Jackson, paraprofessional, Baker Middle School, support staff since 2000; Michael Jolly, administrator, Niles Center, since 2004; Beth Ann Jorgensen, teacher, International Academy East, since 1996; Kathleen Knapp, teacher, Services Building, since 1999; Teresa Kniseley, teacher, elementary vocal, since 1996; Cindy Kolesar, teacher, Hamilton Elementary, since 1974; Jo Kwasny, administrator, Boulan Park Middle School, since 1998; Nancy Lining, teacher, Larson Middle School, since 1986; Julie Marjamaa, teacher, Costello Elementary, since 1985; Ivonne Mastracci, secretary, Troy Union Elementary, support staff since 1999; Teresa McCormack, teacher, Smith Middle School, since 1999; Audra Melton, administrator, Baker Middle School, since 2009; Trudi Motzenbecker, teacher, Wattles Elementary, since 2000; Kathlyn O'Bryan, teacher, Troy High School, since 2005; Susan Ohlert, secretary, Central Office, support staff since 1997; Laurie Pickell, teacher, Martell Elementary, since 1985; Betty Prospal, administrative assistant, Central Office, since 1995; Karen Rockwell, cable services coordinator, Services Building, since 1986; Claudia Rzekpa, teacher, Wass and Martell Elementary Schools, since 1996; Nancy Schleicher, teacher, Hamilton Elementary, since 1979; Trevor Smith, teacher, Troy High School, since 1991; and Mary Thomas, teacher, Wattles, since 1997.

The staging instructions are included in the packet: for approximately twenty minutes before the board meeting all the monitors in the room will display a visual recognition of the district's retirees; a note card will be placed on a chair for each retiree attending; Jordan Harris will read the name of each retiree, their position and length of career in the district; the retiree will come forward and stand near the presentation table when their name is read; and Board President Karl Schmidt will present each retiree with a retirement gift, a clock.

**Recognition 2.D: National Teacher Appreciation Week.** Teacher Appreciation Week was celebrated May 7 through May 11, 2018. The resolution recites that throughout Troy and across the country teachers inspire, nurture and open children's minds to new ideas; that teachers promote and strengthen the principles of democratic equality, develop leaders and encourage critical thinking; that Troy teachers set the bar for excellence in education and continually exceed the highest standards in the profession; and that the goal of Teacher Appreciation Week is to raise national and local awareness of teaching excellence in building a better society — resolving that the district supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 7-11, 2018, and encourages schools and community to appropriately recognize the vital and changing role of teachers in imagining and creating a better future for society.

**Consent minutes: the April 10 workshop.** President Schmidt called it to order at 6:15 p.m. at the Troy Center/IA-East with Mr. Miletti absent. Present besides the Board were Superintendent Machesky, administrators Birmingham, Dziatczak, Griffor, Harris and West, consultant Larry Lobert, and members of the Facilities Study Team Attendance Area Committee — Laura Duzey, Courtney Spangler, Emily Cremers, Victoria King, Lori Bluhm, Veronica Pala, Lori Sisk, Delia Rodi-Barczys and Jeff Frederick — with 1 other member in the audience. The agenda was public communication, the Facilities Study Attendance Area Review Team summary, board professional learning on group norms, and other. It adjourned at 10:08 p.m.

**Consent minutes: the April 17, 2018 regular meeting.** President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. with all seven members present — Fleming, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Miletti, Philippart and Schmidt — administrators Birmingham, Brasington, Duda, Jansen, Dixon, Whan, Roncone, Canfield, Morey, Glasser, Harris and West, and approximately 140 members of the audience. For the Mission Moment on oneTROY autism programming, Barnard principal Melanie Morey invited teachers Erica Conklin and Jennifer Erff to join her, and they invited one of their students to come up along with her mom and therapy dog, Willa. The Board then recognized the 36 outstanding teacher nominees, each receiving congratulations, a certificate of recognition and a plant.

**Treasurer's Report, March 2018.** By fund the report gives General Fund (101) $4,631,730.82, with Total General Fund check disbursements of $4,993,833.82 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $7,613,150.06. Adding ACH debits of $70,536.47, outgoing wire transfers of $3,354,883.06 and P-Card purchases of $172,373.08, with no prior period void disbursements, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $11,210,942.67 — the largest month of the fiscal year to date, driven by the wire transfer total. The middle sections of the packet are the March check register run by fund.

**Consent item 5.D: approving the Oakland Intermediate School District budget for 2018-2019.** In accordance with Section 624 of the Revised School Code, the Troy Board of Education is required to review the proposed Oakland ISD budget and express either its support or disapproval. The resolution recites that Section 624 requires the intermediate school board to submit its proposed budget no later than May 1 of each year to the board of each constituent district for review, and that not later than June 1 of each year the board of each constituent district shall review the proposed budget, adopt a resolution expressing support or disapproval, and submit to the intermediate school board any specific objections and proposed changes.

Troy's resolution expresses support — with a caveat written into the resolution itself. The Board "believes that it is the responsibility of the Intermediate School District to be responsible for its own operations, including adoption of its budget," and "the Troy School District's support of the Oakland Intermediate School District's budget is for the sole purpose of complying with Section 624 of the Revised School Code." The secretary or designee shall forward a copy to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1, 2018, and all conflicting resolutions are rescinded.

The attached Overview of Fiscal Year 2018-2019 Oakland Schools Proposed Budgets sets out the ISD's position. Annual property tax collection is in its fifth year of recovery, with FY 2019 the sixth; the FY 2008 base year tax levy was $216.9 million and the FY 2019 expected tax levy is $186.2 million, $30.7 million less than FY 2008. The recovery table shows fiscal year 2008-09 at -0.0075% with no decline from the base year; fiscal years 2010-2013 at -26.90% cumulative, $141.4 million below base; fiscal years 2014-2017 at 6.96%, $186.1 million below; fiscal year 2017-18 estimated at 2.55%, $36.9 million below; fiscal year 2018-19 at 3.40%, $30.8 million below; fiscal year 2019-20 at 3.50%, $24.3 million below; 2020-21 at 3.50%, $17.5 million below; 2021-22 at 3.50%, $10.5 million below; 2022-23 at 3.50%, $3.3 million below; and fiscal year 2023-24 at 3.50%, at which point the decline from the FY08 base is finally erased — a sixteen-year round trip.

A fund balance target setting protocol is proposed, predicated on known economic liabilities or designated reserves of a specific fund and on a percentage of each fund's operating expenditures. The current protocol sets the General Education Fund and Career Focused Education Fund target at 5% to 10% of expenditures; the draft protocol, described as a policy change currently being discussed with the Board of Education, would set it at 5.5% to 10.5% beginning in FY19, with the range increasing .5% each year until FY23, at which time it would be 7.5% to 12.5%. The Special Education Fund target stays at 5% to 10% of expenditures net of LEA distributions under both. The protocol recognizes the State of Michigan's economic environment, the financial condition of the LEAs, and the aim of maximizing district support through program support, subsidies and distributions.

FY19 budget assumptions across the three major operating funds are: state aid revenue stable, with the exception of the elimination of 147c(2) revenue in FY19; interest income stable; property tax increase of 3.4%, which includes the probability of a Headlee rollback; 61a.1 revenue uncertainties; fee-based revenues stable; a health care cap increase of 3.9%; a salary increase of 1.25% plus steps of approximately .5%; a blended MPSERS rate of 26.16%; and Michigan Tax Tribunal repayments at .25% of budgeted tax revenue.

Oakland Schools' fiscal year 2019 total revenue is $320.7 million, composed of property tax revenue $186.2 million (58%), new grant award funding $73.0 million (23%), other local revenue $31.3 million (10%), state revenue $16.1 million (5%), estimated grant carryover $9.6 million (3%) and other financing sources $4.5 million (1%). Countywide LEA membership, blended public school membership, runs 199,713 in 2009, 197,006 in 2010, 194,738, 193,472, 192,229, 190,471, 188,489, 188,904 and 187,896 in 2018, with annual changes mostly between -0.6% and -1.7% — a county losing students slowly and steadily.

**Personnel: nine administrative appointments.** Each carries a two-year contract issued by the Board.

6.A, Finance Director: Kandice Moynihan, with a comprehensive 15-year career in finance and accounting. She began her career after graduating from Wayne State University as an audit associate for Plante Moran, PLLC, then served as accounting supervisor for Garden City Public Schools before joining Walled Lake Consolidated Schools as finance and purchasing manager. She is a Certified Public Accountant with the State of Michigan and a Certified Financial Officer with Michigan School Business Officials, served on the executive committee for the Oakland County School Business Officials and was president of Oakland County Purchasing Officials. She holds a B.A. in business administration from Wayne State and a Master of Science in Accountancy from Walsh College, and begins June 6, 2018.

6.B, Director, Employee Services: John Pagel, who began teaching fourth and fifth grade with Algonac Community Schools after graduating from the University of Michigan in 1989. In 1996 he became assistant principal at Avondale Middle School, in 2003 assumed additional responsibilities as director of technology for the Avondale School District, and became principal at Avondale's Deerfield Elementary in 2000 before accepting the Martell Elementary principalship in 2016. At Avondale he implemented and integrated more than twenty million dollars of IT software and professional development and participated in successful negotiations of twelve district collective bargaining agreements, serving both as a Board of Education team member and representing the unionized building administration association.

6.C, Director, Athletics, Continuing Education and Enrichment: Tim Fulcher, with an extensive 26-year career in education. He began as a high school mathematics teacher for Hazel Park Schools, then was principal at Webb Elementary School in Hazel Park before joining Troy as Boulan Park Middle School assistant principal; he has served the last eight years as principal at Smith Middle School. He coordinated NCA school improvement teams in creating school mission, vision and goal-selecting processes, and holds a B.S. in mathematics education from Indiana's Taylor University and a Master of Education.

6.D, Special Education Supervisor: Sarah Young, with an 18-year career in education. She began as an elementary school special education teacher at Morse Elementary in Troy and is currently the district's behavior support coordinator, where she has developed processes to bring district-wide communication and clarity and to ensure all stakeholders receive hands-on support from the Special Education Leadership Team. Since 2006 she has been a part-time instructor in the special education graduate program at Oakland University. She holds a B.S. in elementary education from the University of Michigan-Flint, a Master of Education in special education from Oakland University, a graduate certificate in applied behavior analysis from Oakland, and an expected degree in special education administration from Wayne State University in June.

6.E, Director, Early Childhood Programs: Erin Keyser, whose 11-year career began in 2007 as a preschool teacher for Chicago's Loyola University. She moved to San Antonio in 2009 as an instructional facilitator for the Edgewood Intermediate School District, returned to Michigan in 2012 as intervention coordinator and Reading Recovery teacher for Warren Woods Public Schools, and advanced to Early Childhood and Title I Coordinator there, serving as building administrator for more than 300 students across all early childhood programs including the Great Start Readiness Program and Early Childhood Special Education. In August 2015 she joined Troy as a preschool teacher at Morse Elementary, where she implemented High Scope curriculum with an emphasis on best-practice authentic assessment. Her appointment staffs the leadership of the preschool the Board had financed and put out to bid two months earlier.

6.F, Principal, Hill Elementary School: Shari Pawlus, who began teaching third and fifth grade at Scotch Elementary School in West Bloomfield in 2006, accepted a fifth-grade position with Troy at Barnard Elementary in 2012, became a teacher coach working with teachers on instructional strategies aligned to the district goal of creating thinking-centered classrooms, returned to the classroom in 2015 teaching third grade at Bemis, and is currently the reading specialist at Morse Elementary. She created curriculum to build community in the school and district (Sharing Circles), coordinated the student yearbook and student council and coached fifth grade basketball, and holds a B.S. in education from Eastern Michigan University and a Master of Education in educational leadership.

6.G, Principal, Baker Middle School: Jonathan Cross, who started as a special education teacher for the Pontiac City School District in 2005, took a special education teaching position with the Avondale School District in 2006 and advanced to interim assistant principal and athletic director at Avondale Middle School in February 2012, and came to Troy in 2012 as Baker Middle School assistant principal. The recommendation credits him with managing the day-to-day requirements needed to sustain a successful school environment, from continuous school improvement and facilitation of student registration to positive behavior supports and character education. He holds a B.S. in education from Central Michigan University and a Master of Education in educational leadership from Oakland University.

6.H, Principal, Boulan Park Middle School: Anthony Morse, who started as a social studies teacher for Stanwood Community Schools, took a teaching position with Madison District Public Schools in 2002 and advanced to principal and athletic director during the 2008 school year, and came to Troy in 2011 as Boulan Park assistant principal. At Boulan Park he was integral to implementing the professional growth models for all teaching staff, creating the master schedule for all students, and co-developing the Summer Success program for both incoming 9th and 6th grade at-risk students. He holds a B.S. in education from Central Michigan University, a Master in the Art of Teaching from Marygrove College and an Education Specialist degree from Oakland University.

6.I, Principal, Smith Middle School: Christian Mueller, who started as an earth science teacher with the Chicago Public Schools in 2005, joined Madison Public Schools in 2006 and became an assistant principal there in 2012, then moved to Utica Community Schools first as an assistant principal and currently as a middle school principal. He has provided leadership on projects ranging from writing annual reports to compiling and managing data for school improvement and assessing district-wide curriculum, and holds a B.A. in history and a Master of Arts in Teaching from Wayne State University and an Educational Specialist in Leadership degree from Oakland University.

Seven of the nine appointees come from inside the district, and two of the three middle school principalships are filled by that building's own assistant principal. The two vacancies being filled at Smith and Boulan Park trace back through this same packet: Tim Fulcher moves out of the Smith principalship into the athletics directorship, and Jo Kwasny, administrator at Boulan Park since 1998, appears on the retiree list.

**Business 8.A: sinking fund site flooring projects.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on flooring replacement work at Athens High School, International Academy East, Boulan Park Middle School, Larson Middle School, Bemis Elementary School, Martell Elementary School and Wass Elementary School, reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations. The resolution awards the flooring replacement work to Conventional Carpet in the amount of $650,000.00 as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Project Fund.

**Business 8.B: asbestos abatement.** An RFP was issued for competitive bids on asbestos abatement work at Athens High School, International Academy East, Boulan Park Middle School, Larson Middle School and Wass Elementary School, reviewed by Rob Carson and NOVA Environmental, Inc. Carson's April 26, 2018 memorandum to Rick West on Bid 9858 records that the scope is to perform asbestos abatement of floor tile in accordance with all required state and federal laws, that the project is necessary in conjunction with the flooring replacement project, and that the RFP resulted in favorable bid responses and pricing; he recommends the vendor based on qualified low bid per the RFP specifications. The resolution awards the asbestos abatement work to Abatement & Demolition Services in the amount of $37,645.00 as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Project Fund. The two awards are one project: the tile has to come up before the new flooring goes down, and the buildings on the abatement list are a subset of the flooring list.

**Other 10.A: Oakland Schools Board of Education biennial election.** The election is June 4, 2018, voting for two, for six-year terms ending June 30, 2024. Kathy Boike's May 8, 2018 email to constituent district secretaries reports that two individuals have filed for the two open seats: Dr. Theresa Rich and Mr. Marc Katz.

Oakland Schools board members are elected by an electoral body composed of one person designated by the board of each constituent school district. The Revised School Code prescribes that each constituent board must adopt a resolution that designates the person to vote on behalf of the local board, directs the designee which candidate the board supports for each position to be filled, and directs the designee to vote for those individuals; districts shall consider the resolution at not less than one meeting before adopting it. The timeline runs: Oakland Schools receives the list of qualified candidates from the Oakland County Clerk's office and forwards it to constituent superintendents and board secretaries; May 14 through June 1, 2018, each constituent board designates its representative, identifies the ISD candidates it supports and adopts an affirming resolution; June 1 at 4:00 PM, copies of district resolutions are due at the Oakland Schools administrative office; June 4 from 5:30 to 7:30 PM, district representatives attend the Oakland Schools Board of Education open meeting to cast ballots, with no absentee ballots accepted; June 5, notification of results goes to district superintendents and the county clerk; and July 17, 2018, successful candidates take the oath of office at the Oakland Schools organizational meeting.

Candidate qualifications require a registered voter at least 18 years of age, a United States citizen residing within one of Oakland County's school districts, a Michigan resident for at least 30 days and a resident of one of the 28 constituent school districts on or before the 30th day prior to the election; a candidate for the 2018 election may also be currently seated on a local school district board of education. Nominating petitions required a minimum of 40 and no more than 100 valid signatures, circulated on a city or township basis, with a $100 nonrefundable fee available in lieu of a petition, and the last day to file with the County Clerk was Friday, May 4, 2018 at 4:00 p.m. The governing statutes provide that the chairperson of the meeting may accept nominations from the floor if no candidates filed for a position, so the ballot must contain several lines for hand entry of candidates nominated at the meeting.

Read as a whole, the May 2018 packet is the district's turnover meeting. Nearly thirty retirements — including employees hired in 1974, 1979 and 1985 — are recognized in the same sitting that installs nine new administrators, four of them principals, on two-year contracts. The two capital items, $650,000.00 of flooring and $37,645.00 of abatement, are a single summer project split across two resolutions, and the ISD budget item is a statutory formality the Board takes care to say it treats as exactly that.
